claim: Tumor suppressor p53 is the most frequently mutated gene in tumors.
source: Tumor suppressor p53 is the most frequently mutated gene in tumors.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in cancer biology stated in the abstract.

claim: BAG2 promotes mutp53 accumulation and GOF in tumors.
source: Here, we found that BAG2, a protein of Bcl-2 associated athanogene (BAG) family, promotes mutp53 accumulation and GOF in tumors.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study as stated in the abstract.

claim: BAG2 binds to mutp53 and translocates to the nucleus to inhibit the MDM2-mutp53 interaction.
source: Mechanistically, BAG2 binds to mutp53 and translocates to the nucleus to inhibit the MDM2-mutp53 interaction, and MDM2-mediated ubiquitination and degradation of mutp53.
evidence: This mechanistic finding is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: BAG2 inhibits MDM2-mediated ubiquitination and degradation of mutp53.
source: Mechanistically, BAG2 binds to mutp53 and translocates to the nucleus to inhibit the MDM2-mutp53 interaction, and MDM2-mediated ubiquitination and degradation of mutp53.
evidence: This is supported by ubiquitination assays and protein stability experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: BAG2 promotes mutp53 GOF in tumor growth, metastasis and chemoresistance.
source: Thus, BAG2 promotes mutp53 accumulation and GOF in tumor growth, metastasis and chemoresistance.
evidence: This is supported by functional assays including xenograft, metastasis, and chemoresistance experiments.

claim: BAG2 is frequently overexpressed in tumors.
source: BAG2 is frequently overexpressed in tumors.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of multiple tumor databases shown in Figure 7A.

claim: BAG2 overexpression is associated with poor prognosis in patients.
source: BAG2 overexpression is associated with poor prognosis in patients and mutp53 accumulation in tumors.
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis from multiple cancer patient cohorts shown in Figure 7B-E.

claim: BAG2 overexpression is associated with mutp53 accumulation in tumors.
source: BAG2 overexpression is associated with poor prognosis in patients and mutp53 accumulation in tumors.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of colorectal cancer samples shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Trp53 is mutated in over 50% of all tumors.
source: Trp53 is the most frequently mutated gene in human tumors; it is mutated in over 50% of all tumors.
evidence: This is a well-established statistic in cancer biology.

claim: Majority of Trp53 mutations are missense mutations localized in the p53 DNA binding domain (DBD).
source: Majority of Trp53 mutations are missense mutations that are localized in the p53 DNA binding domain (DBD), including several mutational hotspots in tumors (e.g., R175, R248, and R273) (Harris and Hollstein, 1993; Freed-Pastor and Prives, 2012; Muller and Vousden, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Many tumor-associated mutant p53 proteins not only lose the tumor suppressive function of wild-type p53 but also gain new oncogenic activities independently of wtp53.
source: Many tumor-associated mutant p53 (mutp53) proteins not only lose the tumor suppressive function of wild-type p53 (wtp53), but also gain new oncogenic activities independently of wtp53, which is defined as mutp53 gain-of-function (GOF) (Freed-Pastor and Prives, 2012; Muller and Vousden, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on mutp53 GOF.

claim: Mutp53 GOFs include promoting tumor growth, metastasis, chemoresistance and metabolic changes.
source: So far, many mutp53 GOFs have been identified, including promoting tumor growth, metastasis, chemoresistance and metabolic changes (Lang et al., 2004; Olive et al., 2004; Muller et al., 2009; Blandino et al., 2012; Freed-Pastor et al., 2012; Cooks et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: wtp53 protein levels are kept low in normal cells and tissues mainly through proteasomal degradation mediated by E3 ubiquitin ligase MDM2.
source: Under the non-stressed condition, wtp53 protein levels are kept low in normal cells and tissues mainly through the proteasomal degradation mediated by E3 ubiquitin ligase MDM2, the most critical negative regulator for wtp53 (Brooks and Gu, 2006; Hu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature on p53 regulation.

claim: MDM2 is the most critical negative regulator for wtp53.
source: Under the non-stressed condition, wtp53 protein levels are kept low in normal cells and tissues mainly through the proteasomal degradation mediated by E3 ubiquitin ligase MDM2, the most critical negative regulator for wtp53 (Brooks and Gu, 2006; Hu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: MDM2 is a direct transcriptional target of p53.
source: At the same time, as a direct transcriptional target of p53, MDM2 is up-regulated by p53 under both non-stressed and stressed conditions.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about the p53-MDM2 feedback loop.

claim: p53 and MDM2 form a negative feedback loop to tightly regulate p53 protein levels in cells.
source: Thus, p53 and MDM2 forms a negative feedback loop to tightly regulate p53 protein levels in cells.
evidence: This is a well-established regulatory mechanism in p53 biology.

claim: Mutp53 proteins often become stable and accumulate to high levels in tumors.
source: However, mutp53 proteins often become stable and accumulate to high levels in tumors, which is critical for mutp53 GOF in tumorigenesis and contributes greatly to tumor progression (Oren and Rotter, 2010; Li et al., 2011a; Freed-Pastor and Prives, 2012; Muller and Vousden, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mutp53 protein accumulation is critical for mutp53 GOF in tumorigenesis.
source: However, mutp53 proteins often become stable and accumulate to high levels in tumors, which is critical for mutp53 GOF in tumorigenesis and contributes greatly to tumor progression (Oren and Rotter, 2010; Li et al., 2011a; Freed-Pastor and Prives, 2012; Muller and Vousden, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mutp53 protein is kept at low levels in normal tissues but accumulates to very high levels in tumors in R172H or R270H mutp53 knock-in mice.
source: Mutp53 protein is kept at low levels in normal tissues but accumulates to very high levels in tumors (Lang et al., 2004; Olive et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies using mutp53 knock-in mice.

claim: Loss of MDM2 in mutp53 knock-in mice leads to mutp53 protein accumulation in normal tissues, which in turn promotes tumor development.
source: Furthermore, loss of MDM2 in mutp53 knock-in mice leads to mutp53 protein accumulation in normal tissues, which in turn promotes tumor development (Terzian et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: MDM2 retains the ability to degrade mutp53 in in vitro cultured cells.
source: Recent studies including ours also showed that MDM2 retains the ability to degrade mutp53 in in vitro cultured cells (Lukashchuk and Vousden, 2007; Zheng et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies including the authors' own work.

claim: The disruption of MDM2-mediated mutp53 degradation in tumors could be a main cause for the frequently observed mutp53 protein accumulation in tumors.
source: These results strongly suggest that while MDM2 maintains mutp53 protein levels low in normal tissues, the disruption of MDM2-mediated mutp53 degradation in tumors could be a main cause for the frequently observed mutp53 protein accumulation in tumors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies and observations.

claim: BAG2 was identified as a novel mutp53 binding protein using LC-MS/MS assays in tumors from R172H mutp53 knock-in mice.
source: In this study, to investigate the mechanism underlying mutp53 accumulation in tumors, we screened for proteins interacting with mutp53 using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) assays in tumors from R172H mutp53 knock-in mice, and identified BAG2 as a novel mutp53 binding protein that plays a critical role in promoting mutp53 accumulation in tumors.
evidence: This is the main experimental finding described in the introduction.

claim: BAG2 belongs to the Bcl-2 associated athanogene (BAG) family, which is characterized by the BAG domain.
source: BAG2 belongs to the Bcl-2 associated athanogene (BAG) family, which is characterized by the BAG domain.
evidence: This is a factual statement about BAG2 protein family classification.

claim: BAG proteins interact with a variety of proteins and take part in diverse cellular processes, including cell division, cell death and differentiation.
source: As a group of multifunctional proteins, BAG proteins interact with a variety of proteins and take part in diverse cellular processes, including cell division, cell death and differentiation (Takayama and Reed, 2001; Kabbage and Dickman, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on BAG proteins.

claim: Mutp53 binds to BAG2 and promotes the nuclear translocation of BAG2.
source: We found that mutp53 binds to BAG2 and promotes the nuclear translocation of BAG2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The BAG2-mutp53 interaction in the nucleus inhibits the ubiquitination and degradation of mutp53 mediated by MDM2.
source: The BAG2-mutp53 interaction in the nucleus inhibits the ubiquitination and degradation of mutp53 mediated by MDM2, and thereby promotes mutp53 accumulation and mutp53 GOF in tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Knockdown of BAG2 greatly decreases mutp53 protein levels in tumors.
source: Knockdown of BAG2 greatly decreases mutp53 protein levels in tumors and compromises mutp53 GOF in tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 6.

claim: Knockdown of BAG2 compromises mutp53 GOF in tumorigenesis.
source: Knockdown of BAG2 greatly decreases mutp53 protein levels in tumors and compromises mutp53 GOF in tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is supported by functional assays shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: R172H mutp53 knock-in mice mainly develop lymphomas in the spleen and thymus.
source: R172H mutp53 knock-in (Trp53R172H/R172H) mice mainly develop lymphomas in the spleen and thymus (Lang et al., 2004; Olive et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies on these mice.

claim: Mutp53 protein levels are drastically increased in majority of tumors from Trp53R172H/R172H mice but are very low in normal tissues.
source: Mutp53 protein levels are drastically increased in majority of tumors from Trp53R172H/R172H mice but are very low in normal tissues.
evidence: This is an observation from the authors' experiments.

claim: Several known mutp53-binding proteins, including HSP90, Myosin, Cct8 and Pontin, were identified in tumors of Trp53R172H/R172H mice by LC-MS/MS.
source: Several known mutp53-binding proteins, including HSP90, Myosin, Cct8 and Pontin (Muller et al., 2005; Trinidad et al., 2013; Arjonen et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2015), were among the list of proteins identified in tumors of Trp53R172H/R172H mice, which validated our approach.
evidence: This validates the LC-MS/MS approach by identifying known interactors, supported by citations.

claim: The BAG2-mutp53 interaction in Trp53R172H/R172H tumors was confirmed by co-IP followed by Western blot assays.
source: The BAG2-mutp53 interaction in Trp53R172H/R172H tumors was confirmed by co-IP followed by Western blot assays (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Weak interaction between BAG2 and mutp53 was observed in normal tissues from Trp53R172H/R172H mice, including thymus, spleen and kidney.
source: The weak interaction between BAG2 and mutp53 was also observed in normal tissues from Trp53R172H/R172H mice, including thymus, spleen and kidney (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: BAG2 preferentially binds to mutp53 compared with wtp53 in H1299 cells.
source: Co-IP assays employing either anti-p53 or anti-HA antibodies showed that BAG2 preferentially bound to mutp53 compared with wtp53 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Strong BAG2-mutp53 interaction was observed with different mutp53 proteins, including R175H, R248W and R273H.
source: In addition to R175H, the strong BAG2-mutp53 interaction was observed in H1299 cells with ectopic expression of different mutp53 proteins, including R248W and R273H, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Interaction between endogenous BAG2 and mutp53 proteins was observed in several human cancer cell lines.
source: The interaction between the endogenous BAG2 and mutp53 proteins was also observed in several human cancer cell lines, including human colorectal cancer HCT116 p53R248W/−, HT-29 and SW480 cell lines which contain a single copy of Trp53 gene with R248W and R273H mutation, respectively, human breast cancer SK-BR-3, MDA-MB-468 cell lines which contain a single copy of Trp53 gene with R175H and R273H mutation, respectively, and human hepatocellular carcinoma Huh-7 cell lines which contain a single copy of Trp53 gene with Y220C mutation (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: BAG2 is a novel mutp53-specific binding partner, and this interaction is conserved in both mouse tumors and human cancer cells.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that BAG2 is a novel mutp53-specific binding partner, and this interaction is conserved in both mouse tumors and human cancer cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from multiple cell lines and mouse tumors.

claim: BAG2 interacts with mutp53 DNA binding domain (DBD).
source: Results of co-IP assays using an anti-Flag antibody showed that BAG2 interacted with all mutp53 (R175H) fragments containing the mutp53 DBD (P1-P5 in Figure 2D), but not the fragment lacking the mutp53 DBD (P6 in Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by domain mapping experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: BAG2 preferentially binds to DBDs of different mutp53 (R175H, R248W and R273H) but not wtp53 DBD.
source: Furthermore, BAG2 preferentially bound to DBDs of different mutp53 (R175H, R248W and R273H) but not wtp53 DBD (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP experimental data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mutp53 DBD and BAG domain of BAG2 are essential for the BAG2-mutp53 interaction.
source: These results demonstrate that mutp53 DBD and BAG domain of BAG2 are essential for the BAG2-mutp53 interaction.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on domain mapping experiments shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: BAG2 contains a BAG domain (amino acids 91–211) at the C-terminus.
source: BAG2 contains a BAG domain (amino acids 91–211) at the C-terminus (Dai et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a factual statement about BAG2 structure supported by citation.

claim: BAG2 fragments containing the BAG domain interact with mutp53 while the N-terminus of BAG2 protein lacking the BAG domain does not interact with mutp53.
source: The fragments containing the BAG domain interacted with mutp53 while the N-terminus of BAG2 protein lacking the BAG domain did not interact with mutp53 (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by domain mapping experiments shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The binding of mutp53 to the BAG2 fragment which lacks the N-terminus is much weaker compared with the full length BAG2 protein.
source: Interestingly, the binding of mutp53 to the BAG2 fragment which lacks the N-terminus is much weaker compared with the full length (FL) BAG2 protein.
evidence: This is an observation from the domain mapping experiments shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The N-terminus of BAG2 has an additional role for efficient BAG2-mutp53 complex formation although itself does not directly interact with mutp53.
source: It is possible that the N-terminus of BAG2 has an additional role for efficient BAG2-mutp53 complex formation although itself does not directly interact with mutp53.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that the BAG domain alone binds more weakly than full-length BAG2.

claim: BAG2 stabilizes some of its binding proteins, such as PINK1 and ataxin3-80Q.
source: It was reported that BAG2 stabilizes some of its binding proteins, such as PINK1 and ataxin3-80Q (Che et al., 2013, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: BAG2 knockdown greatly decreased mutp53 protein levels in HCT116 p53R248W/− cells and Saos2 cells with stable ectopic expression of different mutp53.
source: While BAG2 knockdown showed no apparent effect on mutp53 mRNA levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), BAG2 knockdown greatly decreased the mutp53 protein levels in cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: BAG2 knockdown showed no apparent effect on mutp53 mRNA levels.
source: While BAG2 knockdown showed no apparent effect on mutp53 mRNA levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), BAG2 knockdown greatly decreased the mutp53 protein levels in cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ectopic BAG2 expression clearly increased mutp53 protein levels.
source: Ectopic BAG2 expression by vectors clearly increased mutp53 protein levels (Figure 3C), while had no clear effect on mutp53 mRNA levels in cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Ectopic BAG2 expression had no clear effect on mutp53 mRNA levels in cells.
source: Ectopic BAG2 expression by vectors clearly increased mutp53 protein levels (Figure 3C), while had no clear effect on mutp53 mRNA levels in cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by real-time PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: BAG2 increases mutp53 protein levels in cells.
source: These results demonstrate that BAG2 increases mutp53 protein levels in cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the knockdown and overexpression experiments shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Blocking proteasomal degradation by MG132 largely abolished the effect of BAG2 knockdown on mutp53 protein levels.
source: We found that blocking proteasomal degradation by the proteasome inhibitor MG132 largely abolished the effect of BAG2 knockdown on mutp53 protein levels in HCT116 p53R248W/−, Saos2-R175H, Saos2-R248W and Saos2-R273H cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Ectopic expression of MDM2 clearly down-regulated mutp53 R175H in H1299 cells co-transfected with vectors expressing mutp53 R175H and MDM2.
source: Ectopic expression of MDM2 clearly down-regulated mutp53 R175H in H1299 cells co-transfected with vectors expressing mutp53 R175H and MDM2 (Figure 3E), which is consistent with previous reports (Lukashchuk and Vousden, 2007; Zheng et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3E and citations to previous studies.

claim: Co-expression of BAG2 largely reduced the degradation of mutp53 protein mediated by MDM2.
source: Notably, co-expression of BAG2 largely reduced the degradation of mutp53 protein mediated by MDM2 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Knockdown of endogenous MDM2 clearly increased mutp53 protein levels in Saos2-R175H cells.
source: Consistently, knockdown of endogenous MDM2 clearly increased mutp53 protein levels in Saoa2-R175H cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The effect of BAG2 knockdown on mutp53 protein levels was greatly reduced in cells with MDM2 knockdown.
source: Notably, the effect of BAG2 knockdown on mutp53 protein levels was greatly reduced in cells with MDM2 knockdown, indicating that the effect of BAG2 knockdown on mutp53 protein levels is largely mediated by MDM2 (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The effect of BAG2 knockdown on mutp53 protein levels is largely mediated by MDM2.
source: Notably, the effect of BAG2 knockdown on mutp53 protein levels was greatly reduced in cells with MDM2 knockdown, indicating that the effect of BAG2 knockdown on mutp53 protein levels is largely mediated by MDM2 (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the MDM2 knockdown rescue experiment shown in Figure 3F.

claim: MDM2 directly binds to mutp53 to negatively regulate mutp53.
source: MDM2 directly binds to mutp53 to negatively regulate mutp53.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MDM2-p53 interaction.

claim: Co-expression of BAG2 clearly decreased the interaction of MDM2 with mutp53 in H1299 cells.
source: Co-expression of BAG2 clearly decreased the interaction of MDM2 with mutp53 in H1299 cells, which could be an important mechanism by which BAG2 inhibits MDM2-mediated mutp53 degradation (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Decreased MDM2-mutp53 interaction by BAG2 could be an important mechanism by which BAG2 inhibits MDM2-mediated mutp53 degradation.
source: Co-expression of BAG2 clearly decreased the interaction of MDM2 with mutp53 in H1299 cells, which could be an important mechanism by which BAG2 inhibits MDM2-mediated mutp53 degradation (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that BAG2 reduces MDM2-mutp53 interaction.

claim: Ectopic BAG2 expression reduced ubiquitination of mutp53 in H1299 cells.
source: Ectopic BAG2 expression reduced ubiquitination of mutp53 in H1299 cells (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Knockdown of endogenous BAG2 by siRNA increased ubiquitination of mutp53 in Saos2-R175H cells.
source: Knockdown of endogenous BAG2 by siRNA increased ubiquitination of mutp53 in Saos2-R175H cells (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: BAG2 interacts with mutp53, and inhibits MDM2 binding to and degradation of mutp53, which leads to mutp53 accumulation in cells.
source: These results demonstrate that BAG2 interacts with mutp53, and inhibits MDM2 binding to and degradation of mutp53, which leads to the mutp53 accumulation in cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: BAG2 proteins were mainly localized in the cytoplasm in H1299 cells with ectopic expression of BAG2 alone.
source: Indeed, in H1299 cells with ectopic expression of BAG2 alone, BAG2 proteins were predominantly localized in the cytoplasm as determined by immunofluorescence (IF) staining (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Mutp53 promoted BAG2 nuclear translocation.
source: Interestingly, we found that mutp53 promoted BAG2 nuclear translocation; ectopic expression of mutp53 (R175H, R248W and R273H), which is mainly localized in the nucleus, clearly increased the translocation of BAG2 from the cytoplasm to the nucleus in cells transfected with vectors expressing BAG2 together with mutp53.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: BAG2 was largely co-localized with mutp53 in the nucleus.
source: Furthermore, BAG2 was largely co-localized with mutp53 in the nucleus (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Ectopic expression of wtp53 did not have an obvious effect on BAG2 nuclear translocation in cells.
source: In contrast, ectopic expression of wtp53, which is also mainly localized in the nucleus, did not have an obvious effect on BAG2 nuclear translocation in cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Both mutp53 and MDM2 proteins contain a nuclear localization signal (NLS) and are mainly localized in the nucleus.
source: Both mutp53 and MDM2 proteins contain a nuclear localization signal (NLS) and are mainly localized in the nucleus, where MDM2 binds to and ubiquitinates mutp53 protein.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mutp53 and MDM2 localization.

claim: MDM2 binds to and ubiquitinates mutp53 protein in the nucleus.
source: Both mutp53 and MDM2 proteins contain a nuclear localization signal (NLS) and are mainly localized in the nucleus, where MDM2 binds to and ubiquitinates mutp53 protein.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MDM2 function.

claim: The translocation of BAG2 to the nucleus where it interacts with mutp53 may play an important role in blocking MDM2 to bind to and degrade mutp53.
source: The translocation of BAG2 to the nucleus where it interacts with mutp53 may play an important role in blocking MDM2 to bind to and degrade mutp53.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that BAG2 translocates to the nucleus with mutp53.

claim: Mutp53NLS proteins were mainly localized in the cytoplasm.
source: Unlike mutp53 proteins which were mainly localized in the nucleus, mutp53NLS proteins were mainly localized in the cytoplasm as shown by IF staining (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Mutp53NLS readily interacted with BAG2.
source: While mutp53NLS readily interacted with BAG2 as determined by co-IP assays (Figure 4C), mutp53NLS could not promote the nuclear translocation of BAG2.
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Mutp53NLS could not promote the nuclear translocation of BAG2.
source: While mutp53NLS readily interacted with BAG2 as determined by co-IP assays (Figure 4C), mutp53NLS could not promote the nuclear translocation of BAG2.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: BAG2 was mainly localized in the cytoplasm in H1299 co-transfected with vectors expressing BAG2 and mutp53NLS.
source: BAG2 was mainly localized in the cytoplasm in H1299 co-transfected with vectors expressing BAG2 and mutp53NLS (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Ectopic expression of MDM2 showed a limited effect on degradation of mutp53NLS protein compared with mutp53 (R175H).
source: Notably, ectopic expression of MDM2 showed a limited effect on degradation of mutp53NLS protein compared with mutp53 (R175H) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Co-expression of BAG2 had no obvious effect on mutp53NLS protein levels in cells co-transfected with expression vectors of BAG2, mutp53NLS and MDM2.
source: Furthermore, co-expression of BAG2 had no obvious effect on mutp53NLS protein levels in cells co-transfected with expression vectors of BAG2, mutp53NLS and MDM2 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Mutp53 promotes BAG2 nuclear localization and the BAG2-mutp53 interaction in the nucleus inhibits MDM2-mediated mutp53 protein degradation.
source: These results strongly suggest that mutp53 promotes BAG2 nuclear localization and the BAG2-mutp53 interaction in the nucleus inhibits MDM2-mediated mutp53 protein degradation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mutp53NLS experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Chemoresistance is one of the most important mutp53 GOFs.
source: Chemoresistance is one of the most important mutp53 GOFs (Napoli et al., 2012; Masciarelli et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: 5-FU induced less apoptosis in Saos2-R175H, Saos2-R248W and Saos2-R273H cells compared with Saos2-Con cells.
source: 5-FU induced less apoptosis in Saos2-R175H, Saos2-R248W and Saos2-R273H cells compared with Saos2-Con cells as determined by Annexin V staining and the levels of cleaved Caspase 3 protein, demonstrating that mutp53 promotes chemoresistance, which is consistent with previous reports (Napoli et al., 2012; Masciarelli et al., 2014) (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by Annexin V and Western blot data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Mutp53 promotes chemoresistance.
source: 5-FU induced less apoptosis in Saos2-R175H, Saos2-R248W and Saos2-R273H cells compared with Saos2-Con cells as determined by Annexin V staining and the levels of cleaved Caspase 3 protein, demonstrating that mutp53 promotes chemoresistance, which is consistent with previous reports (Napoli et al., 2012; Masciarelli et al., 2014) (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claim: Knockdown of BAG2 increased 5-FU-induced apoptosis in Saos2-R175H, Saos2-R248W and Saos2-R273H cells but showed a very limited effect in Saos2-Con cells.
source: Notably, knockdown of BAG2 increased 5-FU-induced apoptosis in Saos2-R175H, Saos2-R248W and Saos2-R273H cells but showed a very limited effect in Saos2-Con cells (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by Annexin V and Western blot data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: 5-FU induced less apoptosis in HCT116 p53R248W/− cells compared with HCT116 p53−/− cells.
source: Consistently, 5-FU induced less apoptosis in HCT116 p53R248W/− cells compared with HCT116 p53−/− cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Knockdown of BAG2 increased 5-FU-induced apoptosis in HCT116 p53R248W/− but not HCT116 p53−/− cells.
source: Knockdown of BAG2 increased 5-FU-induced apoptosis in HCT116 p53R248W/− but not HCT116 p53−/− cells (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is supported by Annexin V and Western blot data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: BAG2, which promotes mutp53 protein accumulation, promotes mutp53 GOF in chemoresistance.
source: These results demonstrate that BAG2, which promotes mutp53 protein accumulation, promotes mutp53 GOF in chemoresistance.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the chemoresistance experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Mutp53 (R175H, R248W and R273H) promoted migration of Saos2 cells compared with p53-null Saos2-Con cells.
source: Compared with p53-null cells (Saos2-Con and HCT116 p53−/− cells), mutp53 (R175H, R248W and R273H in Saos2 cells and R248W in HCT116 p53R248W/− cells) promoted migration of cells as determined by transwell assays (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by transwell assay data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Mutp53 (R248W) promoted migration of HCT116 p53R248W/− cells compared with p53-null HCT116 p53−/− cells.
source: Compared with p53-null cells (Saos2-Con and HCT116 p53−/− cells), mutp53 (R175H, R248W and R273H in Saos2 cells and R248W in HCT116 p53R248W/− cells) promoted migration of cells as determined by transwell assays (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is supported by transwell assay data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Knockdown of BAG2 by either siRNA oligos or shRNA vectors largely abolished the promoting effect of mutp53 on migration in these cells.
source: Notably, knockdown of BAG2 by either siRNA oligos or shRNA vectors largely abolished the promoting effect of mutp53 on migration in these cells (Figure 6A,B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by transwell assay data shown in Figure 6A,B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutp53 (R248W) greatly promoted lung metastatic tumor formation in nude mice.
source: Mutp53 (R248W) greatly promoted lung metastatic tumor formation in nude mice; HCT116 p53R248W/− cells formed significantly higher number and larger size of tumors compared with HCT116 p53−/− cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo metastasis assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Knockdown of BAG2 greatly abolished the promoting effect of mutp53 on lung metastatic tumor formation.
source: Notably, this effect was greatly abolished by knockdown of BAG2 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo metastasis assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: BAG2 promotes mutp53 GOF in metastasis.
source: These results demonstrate that BAG2 promotes mutp53 GOF in metastasis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the migration and metastasis experiments shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: Mutp53 (R248W) promoted proliferation and anchorage-independent growth of HCT116 cells.
source: As shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2, mutp53 (R248W) promoted proliferation and anchorage-independent growth of HCT116 cells.
evidence: This is supported by soft agar and cell counting data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Knockdown of BAG2 clearly inhibited the rates of cell proliferation and anchorage-independent growth in HCT116 p53R248W/− but not HCT116 p53−/− cells.
source: Notably, knockdown of BAG2 clearly inhibited the rates of cell proliferation and anchorage-independent growth in HCT116 p53R248W/− but not HCT116 p53−/− cells.
evidence: This is supported by soft agar and cell counting data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Knockdown of BAG2 in HCT116 p53R248W/− cells significantly inhibited the growth of xenograft tumors.
source: As shown in Figure 6E, knockdown of BAG2 in HCT116 p53R248W/− cells significantly inhibited the growth of xenograft tumors, whereas knockdown of BAG2 in HCT116 p53−/− had much less effect on the growth of xenograft tumors.
evidence: This is supported by xenograft tumor growth data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Knockdown of BAG2 in HCT116 p53−/− had much less effect on the growth of xenograft tumors.
source: As shown in Figure 6E, knockdown of BAG2 in HCT116 p53R248W/− cells significantly inhibited the growth of xenograft tumors, whereas knockdown of BAG2 in HCT116 p53−/− had much less effect on the growth of xenograft tumors.
evidence: This is supported by xenograft tumor growth data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Knockdown of endogenous BAG2 clearly decreased mutp53 protein levels in HCT116 p53R248W/− tumors.
source: Furthermore, knockdown of endogenous BAG2 clearly decreased mutp53 protein levels in HCT116 p53R248W/− tumors as determined by Western blot assays (Figure 6F), which is consistent with the results obtained from in vitro cultured cells.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data from tumor samples shown in Figure 6F.

claim: BAG2 promotes mutp53 GOFs in tumor cell growth.
source: These results demonstrate that BAG2 promotes mutp53 GOFs in tumor cell growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the proliferation, soft agar, and xenograft experiments shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: BAG2 expression was found elevated in many types of human tumors, including colorectal cancers, lung cancers, breast cancers and sarcomas, compared with normal tissues.
source: BAG2 expression was found elevated in many types of human tumors, including colorectal cancers, lung cancers, breast cancers and sarcomas, compared with normal tissues as analyzed in 4 databases from Oncomine (GSE20842, Gaedcke et al., 2011; GSE10072, Landi et al., 2008; GSE3744, Richardson, 2006; GSE21122, Taylor et al., 2010) (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of Oncomine databases shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The amplification of BAG2 was observed in many types of human tumors.
source: The amplification of BAG2 was observed in many types of human tumors as analyzed by employing the cBioportal for Cancer Genomics (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), suggesting that gene amplification is an important mechanism for BAG2 overexpression in tumors.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of cBioportal data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gene amplification is an important mechanism for BAG2 overexpression in tumors.
source: The amplification of BAG2 was observed in many types of human tumors as analyzed by employing the cBioportal for Cancer Genomics (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), suggesting that gene amplification is an important mechanism for BAG2 overexpression in tumors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of BAG2 amplification in tumors.

claim: BAG2 overexpression is associated with poor disease free survival in colorectal cancer patients (HR = 1.40, p = 0.022).
source: As shown in Figure 7B–E, BAG2 overexpression is associated with poor disease free survival in colorectal cancer patients (HR = 1.40, p = 0.022), poor disease specific survival in lung cancer patients (HR = 2.4, p = 0.00001), poor relapse free survival in breast cancer patients (HR = 1.3, p = 0.00014) and poor distant recurrence free survival in soft tissue cancer patients (HR = 1.67, p = 0.00001).
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: BAG2 overexpression is associated with poor disease specific survival in lung cancer patients (HR = 2.4, p = 0.00001).
source: As shown in Figure 7B–E, BAG2 overexpression is associated with poor disease free survival in colorectal cancer patients (HR = 1.40, p = 0.022), poor disease specific survival in lung cancer patients (HR = 2.4, p = 0.00001), poor relapse free survival in breast cancer patients (HR = 1.3, p = 0.00014) and poor distant recurrence free survival in soft tissue cancer patients (HR = 1.67, p = 0.00001).
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: BAG2 overexpression is associated with poor relapse free survival in breast cancer patients (HR = 1.3, p = 0.00014).
source: As shown in Figure 7B–E, BAG2 overexpression is associated with poor disease free survival in colorectal cancer patients (HR = 1.40, p = 0.022), poor disease specific survival in lung cancer patients (HR = 2.4, p = 0.00001), poor relapse free survival in breast cancer patients (HR = 1.3, p = 0.00014) and poor distant recurrence free survival in soft tissue cancer patients (HR = 1.67, p = 0.00001).
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: BAG2 overexpression is associated with poor distant recurrence free survival in soft tissue cancer patients (HR = 1.67, p = 0.00001).
source: As shown in Figure 7B–E, BAG2 overexpression is associated with poor disease free survival in colorectal cancer patients (HR = 1.40, p = 0.022), poor disease specific survival in lung cancer patients (HR = 2.4, p = 0.00001), poor relapse free survival in breast cancer patients (HR = 1.3, p = 0.00014) and poor distant recurrence free survival in soft tissue cancer patients (HR = 1.67, p = 0.00001).
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: BAG2 expression levels have significant prognostic value for patients with various types of cancer.
source: These results suggest the significant prognostic value of BAG2 expression levels for patients with various types of cancer.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the survival analysis data shown in Figure 7B-E.

claim: There is a clear correlation between high BAG2 expression and mutp53 accumulation in colorectal tumors.
source: There is a clear correlation between high BAG2 expression and mutp53 accumulation (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of colorectal cancer samples shown in Figure 7F.

claim: In tumors with mutp53, 66.7% of tumors with high BAG2 expression displayed high p53 staining while only 40.9% tumors with low BAG2 expression had high p53 staining (p = 0.035).
source: In tumors with mutp53, 66.7% of tumors (18 out of 27) with high BAG2 expression displayed high p53 staining (>30% cells are stained) while only 40.9% tumors (9 out of 22) with low BAG2 expression had high p53 staining (p = 0.035).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of colorectal cancer samples shown in Figure 7F.

claim: In tumors with wtp53, there is no correlation between BAG2 expression and p53 accumulation.
source: In contrast, in tumors with wtp53, there is no correlation between BAG2 expression and p53 accumulation.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of colorectal cancer samples shown in Figure 7F.

claim: BAG2 overexpression is significantly correlated with accumulation of mutp53 protein in colorectal cancers.
source: These results demonstrate that BAG2 overexpression is significantly correlated with accumulation of mutp53 protein in colorectal cancers.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of colorectal cancer samples shown in Figure 7F.

claim: MDM2 maintains mutp53 protein levels low in normal tissues.
source: Results from mouse genetic experiments with knockout of MDM2 in mutp53 mice and cell-based in vitro experiments suggest that MDM2 maintains mutp53 protein levels low in normal tissues, whereas some changes occurred in tumors disrupt MDM2-mediated mutp53 degradation, thereby leading to mutp53 accumulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited mouse genetic and cell-based experiments.

claim: Some changes occurred in tumors disrupt MDM2-mediated mutp53 degradation, thereby leading to mutp53 accumulation.
source: Results from mouse genetic experiments with knockout of MDM2 in mutp53 mice and cell-based in vitro experiments suggest that MDM2 maintains mutp53 protein levels low in normal tissues, whereas some changes occurred in tumors disrupt MDM2-mediated mutp53 degradation, thereby leading to mutp53 accumulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited mouse genetic and cell-based experiments.

claim: HSP90 can bind to mutp53 and reduce mutp53 degradation mediated by MDM2.
source: Recent studies have reported that HSP90 can bind to mutp53 and reduce mutp53 degradation mediated by MDM2.
evidence: This is a statement about published findings.

claim: Knockdown of HSP90 by siRNA or blocking HDAC6-HSP90 axis by SAHA induced destabilization of mutp53 and inhibited its GOF in tumorigenesis.
source: Knockdown of HSP90 by siRNA or blocking HDAC6-HSP90 axis by SAHA induced destabilization of mutp53 and inhibited its GOF in tumorigenesis (Li et al., 2011a, 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Tumor-derived MDM2 short isoforms inhibited full-length MDM2-mediated mutp53 degradation, which promoted mutp53 accumulation and enhanced GOF in tumorigenesis.
source: Our recent study showed that tumor-derived MDM2 short isoforms inhibited full-length MDM2-mediated mutp53 degradation, which promoted mutp53 accumulation and enhanced GOF in tumorigenesis (Zheng et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous study.

claim: The BAG domain is a conserved region located at the C-terminus of the BAG-family proteins that binds to the ATPase domain of Hsc70 and has general nucleotide exchange activities towards Hsc70.
source: The BAG domain is a conserved region located at the C-terminus of the BAG-family proteins that binds to the ATPase domain of Hsc70 and has general nucleotide exchange activities towards Hsc70 (Takayama and Reed, 2001; Kabbage and Dickman, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on BAG domain function.

claim: Proteins containing the BAG domain often function as a co-chaperone protein.
source: Therefore, proteins containing the BAG domain often functions as a co-chaperone protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of the BAG domain.

claim: BAG2 interacts with and stabilizes PINK1 and ataxin3-80Q through inhibiting their ubiquitination and degradation.
source: Recently, it was reported that BAG2 interacts with and stabilizes PINK1 and ataxin3-80Q, proteins involved in neurological diseases, through inhibiting their ubiquitination and degradation (Che et al., 2013, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: BAG2 can deliver Tau to the proteasome for protein degradation independently of ubiquitination.
source: BAG2 can also deliver Tau to the proteasome for protein degradation independently of ubiquitination (Carrettiero et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: BAG2 can interact with many different mutp53, including several tumor-associated mutational hotspots.
source: In this study, we found that BAG2 preferentially binds to mutp53 at the DBD domain. BAG2 can interact with many different mutp53, including several tumor-associated mutational hotspots.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The BAG2-mutp53 interaction is conserved in both human tumor cells and mouse tissues.
source: This BAG2-mutp53 interaction is conserved in both human tumor cells and mouse tissues.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from both human cells and mouse tissues shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Conformational changes of mutp53 proteins may lead to its association with chaperone and co-chaperone proteins.
source: It is possible that conformational changes of mutp53 proteins lead to its association with chaperone and co-chaperone proteins.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of BAG2-mutp53 interaction.

claim: Targeting BAG2 could be developed as a novel strategy to destabilize mutp53 and inhibit its GOF in tumorigenesis.
source: These results strongly suggest that targeting BAG2 could be developed as a novel strategy to destabilize mutp53 and inhibit its GOF in tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion and suggestion based on the experimental findings.

claim: BAG2 plays an important role in tumorigenesis.
source: These results strongly suggest that BAG2 plays an important role in tumorigenesis and promoting mutp53 accumulation and GOF is a novel mechanism for BAG2 in tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings showing BAG2's effects on tumor growth, metastasis, and chemoresistance.

claim: Promoting mutp53 accumulation and GOF is a novel mechanism for BAG2 in tumorigenesis.
source: These results strongly suggest that BAG2 plays an important role in tumorigenesis and promoting mutp53 accumulation and GOF is a novel mechanism for BAG2 in tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Less than 10% of tumors had the amplification of BAG2 in majority of tumor types.
source: Considering that less than 10% of tumors had the amplification of BAG2 in majority of tumor types, it is possible that additional mechanisms contribute to BAG2 overexpression in tumors, which needs further investigation in future studies.
evidence: This is an observation from the cBioportal analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Additional mechanisms may contribute to BAG2 overexpression in tumors.
source: Considering that less than 10% of tumors had the amplification of BAG2 in majority of tumor types, it is possible that additional mechanisms contribute to BAG2 overexpression in tumors, which needs further investigation in future studies.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that amplification alone cannot explain all BAG2 overexpression.

claim: Trp53 is the most frequently-mutated gene in tumors.
source: Considering that BAG2 is frequently overexpressed in cancer cells, our findings revealed a new and important mechanism for mutp53 protein accumulation in tumors. Trp53 is the most frequently-mutated gene in tumors.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in cancer biology.

claim: Mutp53 protein is frequently accumulated in tumors, which is critical for mutp53 GOF in tumor development.
source: Mutp53 protein is frequently accumulated in tumors, which is critical for mutp53 GOF in tumor development.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the literature cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: Mutp53 has become an extremely attractive target for tumor therapy.
source: Therefore, mutp53 has become an extremely attractive target for tumor therapy.
evidence: This is a statement about the therapeutic potential of targeting mutp53.

claim: BAG2 could be a potential target for cancer therapy in tumors containing mutp53.
source: Our findings that BAG2 promotes mutp53 protein accumulation and mutp53 GOF in tumorigenesis strongly suggest that BAG2 could be a potential target for cancer therapy in tumors containing mutp53.
evidence: This is a conclusion and suggestion based on the experimental findings.
